Cluster tables that hold the same data and propose a canonical member

Source: R/clusters.R
cluster_tables.Rd

Artefact 3 of the roadmap, from profile statistics alone. Columns are matched across tables by what they hold (complete value sets for small code lists, value ranges, distinct rate, value shape, string lengths, and name as a secondary signal), table pairs are scored by how much of each table's information is found in the other, each related pair is labelled (copy, filtered subset, aggregate, wider derivative, related), related tables are grouped into clusters, and a canonical member is proposed for each cluster with a one-line rationale. Every table also gets a class (event, reference, aggregate or other) from its own shape.

Usage

cluster_tables(
  profile,
  inventory,
  min_column_score = 0.7,
  min_containment = 0.75,
  schema_priority = NULL,
  decisions = NULL
)

Arguments

profile

A column_profile covering every table, from a full (unsampled) run.

inventory

The matching db_inventory, for row counts, column counts and freshness.

min_column_score

Lowest column similarity that counts as a match.

min_containment

Lowest containment that makes two tables related.

schema_priority

Optional character vector of schemas in order of preference for the canonical member, for example c("layer1", "derived") to prefer source tables over cleaned copies. Tables in schemas not listed rank after those listed.

decisions

Optional data frame of reviewed decisions, as read by read_cluster_decisions(); confirmed and rejected rows override the proposals.

Value

A list with three tibbles: clusters (one row per table: cluster_id, table, table_class, role, canonical, confidence, rationale, status), pairs (the evidence for every related pair) and matches (the column matches behind the pairs).

Details

The proposals are a starting point for the warehouse owners to confirm, not a verdict: see write_cluster_decisions() for the review file. Clustering needs exact statistics, so it refuses a profile in which any table was sampled.

Scoring

Two columns of the same type class score between 0 and 1 on the evidence available for both: Jaccard overlap of complete value sets (weight 0.5), overlap of ranges or, for suppressed identifiers, of string lengths (0.3), closeness of distinct rate (0.2), overlap of value shapes (0.15) and name similarity (0.15); missing components are left out and the weights rescaled. A match needs a score of at least min_column_score. Columns are weighted by information content (log10 of distinct count), so a shared two-value flag counts for little and a shared identifier for a lot. For a pair of tables, a greedy best-match assignment gives contain_a_in_b (the share of A's information found in B), the reverse, and similarity (their harmonic mean). Pairs with containment of at least min_containment in either direction are related. Copy, subset, wider and narrower also need a shared entity: a matched column that is near-unique and mostly populated in both tables, so a table that merely references this one through a foreign key is not mistaken for a copy. When that shared column has identical values in both tables (equal fingerprints) the rows are known to be the same rows, and the containment threshold drops to 0.5 to allow for renamed or recomputed columns. Two reference tables additionally need a word in common in their names.

Labels

With A the table being described and B the other:

  • copy: containment at least min_containment both ways and row counts within 10 per cent; or an identical identifier column (equal fingerprints) with row counts within 10 per cent, which makes the pair a copy, wider derivative or narrower by column count alone;

  • filtered_subset: A's information is in B, B's is not all in A, and A has fewer rows;

  • wider_derivative: B's information is in A, A has more columns, rows within 10 per cent;

  • narrower: A's information is in B, which has more columns, rows within 10 per cent (the other side of a wider derivative);

  • aggregate: A is of class aggregate and its grouping columns are found in B, which has more rows;

  • related: anything else above the thresholds.

Canonical member

Within a cluster, unless schema_priority decides it, the canonical member is the one with the highest score from: a primary key candidate (+2), lowest grain (log10 rows), width (log10 informative columns), freshness (rank of newest datetime, up to +1), and penalties for being a filtered subset (-3) or aggregate (-5) of another member.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
con <- fakehospdata::fh_connect("sample")
inv <- db_inventory(con, exclude = "^answers\\\\.", progress = FALSE)
prof <- db_profile(con, inv, sample_rows = Inf, progress = FALSE)
cl <- cluster_tables(prof, inv)
cl$clusters[cl$clusters$role != "standalone", ]
} # }
